Nuno Felix RT @Teoyaomiquu : It is worth explaining why 720,000 russian military deaths over nearly five years of war matter much more than many think. An ordinary russian may not give a fuck about these 720,000 dead. Many would say, well, it was their choice. Some see it as tragic, some feel for them, but much of the general population appears indifferent. A large proportion of these troops signed contracts voluntarily in exchange for money. There is a very different perception of their deaths in society. "Your choice, you knew the risks, you took them, and now you are dead. Sorry, but that's the way it is." So let's look at recruitment numbers. Russian budget data shows that the regional cost of recruiting a soldier increased by approximately 36% year over year in October, while recruitment fell by 11% over the first ten months of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025. They are offering more but getting less. This is an obvious indicator of the exhaustion of their existing recruitment pools. There are two main reasons why I think we are seeing this: Information about losses becomes more accessible every day. More people lose family members, more wounded soldiers return home, and more soldiers tell their families what is actually happening on the battlefield. This information spreads through society. The low-hanging fruit of recruitment is gradually disappearing. Those in financial desperation, those heavily in debt, highly motivated patriots, criminals and others for whom military service was an attractive option have already been heavily recruited. Every new recruit costs more and is harder to get. The longer this continues, the more difficult recruitment becomes. Fine, but russia still recruits large numbers of people and manages to fill gaps in its military rosters. That is correct. However, these are just numbers on paper. A brigade of 3,000 soldiers can be an effective, cohesive fighting force, or it can be a demoralized, unwilling and dysfunctional formation that struggles to accomplish even basic tasks. Both look identical on paper. That's where we turn to evidence from the battlefield. We have good mappers such as DeepState, Andrew Perpetua and Clément Molin, who do an excellent job documenting the frontline. Russian territorial gains have significantly decreased, while the number of russian soldiers dying for each square kilometer gained has increased. Estimated deaths per square kilometer: 2025: 60 2026: 120–180 (data is not yet complete) 60 deaths per square kilometer is already an extremely high price to pay. At 120 or even 180, we are talking about an entirely different level of attrition. At this rate, taking the remaining 5,300 square kilometers of Donetsk Oblast controlled by Ukraine would theoretically cost russia another 636,000 to 954,000 military deaths. That's why Ukraine refuses to withdraw. You want it, you pay for it with blood. Why did this number spike so much in 2026? Obviously, Ukraine adapts. Technology evolves,

Nuno Felix RT @Teoyaomiquu: It is worth explaining why 720,000 russian military deaths over nearly five years of war matter much more than many think. An ordinary russian may not give a fuck about these 720,000 dead. Many would say, well, it was their choice.… ld has limits to how many casualties it can sustain without meaningful achievements. No, this is not necessarily the point when a commander says, "I won't send my troops to die anymore." Commanders themselves may become indifferent to the lives of their soldiers. It is the point at which the force loses cohesion and effectiveness. Soldiers become unwilling to fight, desertion increases, trust in commanders disappears, and the formation becomes increasingly ineffective despite being fully staffed. We have seen elements of this during the collapse of the russian imperial army in WWI, during the First Chechen War, and during the collapse of russian defensive positions in Kharkiv Oblast in September 2022. We shouldn't forget Prigozhin's mutiny in June 2023 either. Months of fighting in Bakhmut, enormous losses, growing resentment towards military leadership and public accusations against the Ministry of Defense eventually culminated in an armed rebellion. That happened less than a year and a half into the full-scale war. Think about how much psychological exhaustion, resentment and frustration could have accumulated within the russian military since then. Yes, Ukraine also suffers casualties and has a much smaller manpower pool. But there is a fundamental difference between enduring losses while defending your own country and repeatedly sacrificing thousands of men for another few hundred meters of someone else's land. Under normal circumstances, military leadership facing these diminishing returns would have strong reasons to reconsider its offensive strategy, consolidate its defenses and seek a diplomatic solution. However, I believe putin is politically trapped. While the war continues, the final cost of the war isn't being calculated, the promised rewards are still within reach, and the military remains occupied with fighting. Even a ceasefire could present a serious political risk to putin. Soldiers would have time to reflect on what happened. Society would have more opportunities to ask what was achieved, what was lost, who is responsible, and whether it was worth it. Continuing the war postpones these questions but makes the eventual answers increasingly difficult. And so the meat grinder continues. In my view, the russian military is on a path towards a disaster that cannot simply be prevented by increasing signing bonuses and recruiting more people. Lower oil revenues and Ukrainian deep strikes into russia can further accelerate this process. You can replace dead soldiers. You cannot buy back years of accumulated combat experience, mutual trust, unit cohesion, morale and the willingness to fight. tweet
